groups.content:
The history of canned food

1795, France

  • A prize was offered for a way of preserving food for [1].

1810, France

  • Appert sealed food in glass bottles using cork and [2], then heated them.

1860s, France

  • Pasteur explained that food goes bad because of [3].

1813, London

  • The first canning factory was opened by two [4].

Early nineteenth century

  • Cans were difficult to open; instructions suggested using a hammer and a [5].

1870, USA

  • A safer can opener used a [6] to cut the lid.

1897, USA

  • Removing most of the [7] from soup allowed it to be sold more cheaply.

groups.instruction:
Questions 27-33

Look at the following statements (Questions 27-33) and the list of experts below.

Match each statement with the correct expert, A, B or C.

NB You may use any letter more than once.

List of Experts
A   Alan Whitford
B   Sofia Lindqvist
C   Ruth Adebayo

Questions 34-36

Complete each sentence with the correct ending, A-D, below.

A   the cost of caring for an ageing population.
B   the importance of good health rather than a longer life.
C   who would benefit from new treatments.
D   the effect of longer lives on the natural world.

questions.explanation: Answer: troops Paragraph 2: the French government offered a prize to anyone who could find 'a better way of preserving food for its troops '.
Answer: wax Paragraph 2: Appert would 'seal them tightly with cork and wax , and then heat the bottles in boiling water'.
Answer: microorganisms Paragraph 3: Pasteur 'showed that food is spoiled by microorganisms '. 'Goes bad' paraphrases 'is spoiled'.

Answer: engineers Paragraph 4: Durand's patent was acquired by 'two engineers , Bryan Donkin and John Hall, who opened a canning factory in London in 1813'. Durand himself was a merchant who does not seem to have made cans.
Answer: chisel Paragraph 5: instructions 'advised users to cut around the top with a chisel and hammer'. Bayonets and knives were what soldiers sometimes used, not what the instructions suggested.
Answer: wheel Paragraph 6: 'A much safer design, which used a rotating wheel to cut the lid, appeared in 1870'. The 1858 opener used a curved blade.
Answer: water Paragraph 9: a chemist 'developed a way of removing most of the water from soup, so that the product could be sold in smaller cans at a lower price'.
Answer: NOT GIVEN Paragraph 2 says that Appert 'was eventually awarded the prize in 1810' and published a book, but it gives no information about what he did with the money.
Answer: TRUE Paragraph 4: glass bottles ' broke easily , which made them unsuitable for use on ships or on the battlefield '.
Answer: FALSE Paragraph 4: 'Durand does not appear to have manufactured any cans himself '. His patent was acquired by others.
Answer: FALSE Paragraph 6: 'it was almost fifty years before anyone invented a tool designed specifically for opening cans'. The patent for cans dates from 1810 and the first opener from 1858.
Answer: TRUE Paragraph 7: some historians suggest lead poisoning, but ' The theory remains controversial , however, and other researchers believe that cold, hunger and disease were the main causes'.
Answer: NOT GIVEN Paragraph 9 says that condensed soup 'was an enormous commercial success', but it does not compare its popularity in cities and rural areas.
Answer: v Section A describes the new Amphibian House, which 'is intended to do two things ': make people love amphibians, and show that they are disappearing and what scientists are doing about it.
Answer: ii Section B explains that ' their bodies make them unusually sensitive ': permeable skin, a double life in water and on land, and eggs without a hard shell.
Answer: i Section C: amphibians are often called 'canaries in the coal mine', but ' Not all biologists are happy with the comparison ', and Hargreaves explains why.
Answer: vi Section D lists habitat loss, a fungal disease, climate change and pollution. These are several threats of different kinds. Heading iv (a single cause) is contradicted by this list.
Answer: vii Section E: 'a team of scientists is working to reduce these threats ', testing bacteria against the fungus, water temperature and breeding techniques.
Answer: iii Section F: species thought to be lost have returned to the wild, and Osei says ' We want every visitor to leave believing that these animals have a future. '

text.en: the introduction of predatory fish
the collection of frogs for the pet trade
chemicals used in agriculture
increased levels of noise
the drying out of breeding sites

questions.explanation: Answer: C, E Section D: climate change ' dry out the ponds and streams in which amphibians breed ' (E), and ' Pollution from farm chemicals adds further pressure' (C). Predatory fish, the pet trade and noise are not mentioned.

text.en: creating new wetland habitats near the zoo
using bacteria to help frogs resist disease
training local people to monitor frog populations
recreating weather conditions that trigger breeding
developing a vaccine against the fungus

questions.explanation: Answer: B, D Section E: one project treats frogs ' with beneficial bacteria ' to protect them from the fungus (B), and ' we have built a system that imitates a tropical storm ' because some species breed only after heavy rain (D). A vaccine (E) is not mentioned.
Answer: oxygen Section B: 'many species absorb water and even part of the oxygen they need through it', meaning through their skin.
Answer: insects Section C: 'In many forests, they eat vast numbers of insects '. 'Large quantities' paraphrases 'vast numbers'.
Answer: skin Section D: 'a fungal disease called chytridiomycosis, which attacks the skin '.

Answer: A (Alan Whitford) Paragraph 1: Whitford said that treatments ' should first be tested on people who were already ill , rather than being sold to wealthy customers who simply want to stay young'.

Answer: C (Ruth Adebayo) Paragraph 8: 'Adebayo, by contrast, argued that the fears about overpopulation were exaggerated ', because birth rates are falling. Whitford holds the opposite view (paragraph 7).
Answer: A (Alan Whitford) Paragraph 3: Whitford predicted that ' it would be at least several decades before anything could be said to slow ageing itself'.

Answer: B (Sofia Lindqvist) Paragraph 4: Lindqvist believes that 'a large proportion of the gains still available will come from reducing inequalities in health within countries, rather than from new technology '.
Answer: C (Ruth Adebayo) Paragraph 5: Adebayo argued that this attitude is harmful ' because people who fear getting old often avoid thinking about how they would like to live when they are old '.
Answer: B (Sofia Lindqvist) Paragraph 6: Lindqvist added that ' longer working lives were not necessarily a bad thing '.
Answer: A (Alan Whitford) Paragraph 9: Whitford tells his students that ancient myths contain ' better warnings about science than many scientific papers '.
Answer: B Whitford wants to keep people 'healthy for longer' rather than making them live to 150, and Lindqvist ' agreed that the priority should be health rather than length of life '.

Answer: C Adebayo: ' We should be very careful about whose lives are being extended ', because only the rich might afford treatments. Whitford objects to treatments 'being sold to wealthy customers who simply want to stay young'. Both are concerned about who benefits.
Answer: D Whitford worries that a growing population ' would put even more pressure on resources ', but Adebayo argues that 'the fears about overpopulation were exaggerated'.

text.en: It has increased as scientific knowledge has improved.
It reflects a tendency to regard ageing as an illness.
It is based on a misunderstanding of how the body ages.
It shows that older people are more valued than before.

questions.explanation: Answer: B Paragraph 5: the enthusiasm 'says more about modern attitudes to old age than about science', and ' We have come to see ageing as a disease, something to be cured '. D is the opposite: older people are treated 'as a problem to be solved'.

text.en: They should be managed by private companies.
They have always been too generous.
They were not designed for people living so long after retirement.
They encourage people to stop working too early.

questions.explanation: Answer: C Paragraph 6: 'many pension systems were designed at a time when people rarely lived more than a few years after retiring '.

text.en: Myths about ageing are more popular than scientific explanations.
A longer life without continued health would be undesirable.
Ancient cultures had a surprisingly accurate understanding of ageing.
Students should read more literature as part of their studies.

questions.explanation: Answer: B Paragraph 9: Tithonus ' was granted eternal life but not eternal youth , and so grew older and weaker for ever', and Whitford says 'That is precisely the outcome we need to avoid'. So a long life without health is undesirable.

text.en: warning that myths can give a misleading view of science
explaining why myths about death are similar across cultures
recommending that people's experiences recorded in myths are considered
arguing that scientists should stop researching ageing

questions.explanation: Answer: C Adebayo says myths 'record what people in many different times and places have felt about death', and ' we need to listen to that experience as well as to the scientists '. This is a recommendation. She does not ask scientists to stop their research (D).
